title: A new national team: S. Mallesham and Surendra Kumar Pandey elected
author: Editorial Desk
summary: The BMS 2026-29 national team announced after the Puri conference: who was named, what was resolved, and the agenda ahead.
body:
*Photo: BMS new national leadership, February 2026*

In February 2026 the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS) announced the office-bearers who will lead it for the term **2026–2029**. The announcement came at the close of the organisation's three-day triennial national conference, held in Puri, Odisha, from 6 to 8 February 2026. For an organisation that describes itself as India's largest central trade union, a change of national team is a significant moment. This post sets out who was named, how the conference works, what it resolved, and what the new team will have to deal with.

## Where the announcement came from

According to a report published by *Organiser* on 10 February 2026, the new national committee was elected at the conference in Puri, with delegates present from across the country. The same report records that the conference adopted four major resolutions, which are to be forwarded to the Central Government. BMS has since described the gathering as its 21st All India Conference. The leadership was announced at the end of those three days, and the term runs for three years, until 2029.

## The office-bearers named in the announcement

The report lists the principal office-bearers as follows:

- **President:** Shri S. Mallesham (Telangana)
- **General Secretary:** Shri Surendra Kumar Pandey (Chhattisgarh)
- **Finance Secretary:** Shri Anish Mishra (Delhi)
- **Organising Secretary:** Shri B. Surendran
- **Joint Organising Secretary:** Shri Ganesh Mishra
- **Office Secretary:** Shri Paljeet Parmar

The committee also includes **seven Vice Presidents**, drawn from Punjab, Vidarbha, Uttar Pradesh, Kerala, Rajasthan, Delhi and Gujarat, and **seven Secretaries**, drawn from Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Haryana, Maharashtra and Bihar. The spread of home States is worth noticing. A national union whose affiliates are found in every State and in dozens of industries needs a leadership that reflects that geography, and the list above does so. The full committee is on the *Who's Who* page of this website.

## How BMS is built, and how leadership changes

The Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh was founded on **23 July 1955** at Bhopal under the leadership of Shri Dattopant Thengadi. Its own "At a Glance" note says it began with no union, no member, no office and no funds, and that it did not arise from a split in any existing union. Its first All India Conference was held in Delhi in 1967, where the first national executive was elected; Shri Babasaheb Kambleji became the first President and Thengadi Ji the General Secretary.

The structure is a pyramid. At the base are affiliated unions in individual establishments and industries. They come together in State-level committees and in industry-wise federations. The BMS website lists thirty-eight federations, from the Anganwadi, ASHA, Beedi, Construction and Contract workers' federations to those for railways, ports and docks, banks, plantations and the defence sector. At the top is the national body, whose office-bearers are chosen by delegates at the national conference at a fixed interval of three years.

This regular rhythm matters. The recognition of a union by the Government has long depended on verified membership, and BMS records that in the government verification declared in 1996 it was found to be the largest central trade union organisation, with 31,17,324 members, having been second-largest in 1984. The organisation today describes its membership as close to one crore, with more than 5,000 affiliated unions across all States. These are the organisation's own figures, but they explain why each change of leadership is watched closely by workers, employers and governments. The orderly handover of responsibility at set intervals is a sign of an institution that does not depend on a single person.

## What the Puri conference resolved

The four resolutions give the clearest picture of what the new team has been asked to pursue. As reported:

1. **Universal application of labour laws.** The central demand is that labour laws apply to all workers without exclusion, whatever the sector, type of employment or contractual status. BMS links this to its guiding idea of *Antyodaya*, the upliftment of the last and most marginalised worker. It also asks for a new labour policy that guarantees a living wage and social security to every worker.
2. **Employee status for Anganwadi workers.** BMS argues that Anganwadi workers perform statutory duties under government schemes and should be recognised as government employees, with wages, provident fund, pension, health insurance and gratuity, rather than being treated as volunteers.
3. **Revival of the tripartite mechanism.** BMS says forums where government, employers and unions sit together, such as the Indian Labour Conference, have become irregular, and it asks for regular, outcome-oriented dialogue.
4. **An end to exploitation of contract workers.** The resolution asks for equal pay for equal work, social security, protection from arbitrary termination, and accountability of principal employers.

## The early agenda: protest day and the codes

Within days of the conference, the General Secretary issued a call for a nationwide **Protest Day on 25 February 2026**. District-level dharnas, rallies, gate meetings and the wearing of black badges were planned, with memoranda to be sent through district authorities to the Prime Minister, the Union Labour Minister and Chief Ministers. The grievances listed included low honorariums for mid-day meal and ASHA workers, unpaid or part-paid wages in certain public sector undertakings, the unchanged minimum EPS-95 pension of ₹1,000 (with a demand to raise it to ₹7,500), a five-day week in banking, and higher eligibility ceilings for ESI, EPF and bonus. The call also asked for strict enforcement of labour laws and for corrections in the Industrial Relations Code and the OSH Code.

That last point places the new team in a particular moment. The Government brought the four Labour Codes into effect on 21 November 2025, consolidating 29 central laws. The rules and schemes that give the Codes practical shape are still being consulted upon. For a union, the difference between a good law and a good outcome often lies in those rules, so the team's work with the Labour Ministry in the coming months will matter greatly.

## The international task: the BRICS Trade Union Forum

India holds the BRICS chair in 2026, and the BRICS Trade Union Forum is to be hosted by BMS. Later reports state that the summit is scheduled for 14–16 July 2026 in Hyderabad, that President S. Mallesham leads it, and that a secretariat was inaugurated at BMS headquarters in the presence of the Secretary of the Ministry of Labour & Employment. Four working groups were set up: social security; skilling, reskilling and upskilling; women and the future of work; and human-centric technology and artificial intelligence. Hosting trade unions from several large economies is a large organisational task, and it gives Indian workers' concerns a platform.

## What remains to be done

The new team inherits several unfinished matters at once. Scheme workers still seek recognition and a decent wage. Contract workers form a large and growing share of the factory workforce. Gig and platform workers have been recognised in law for the first time, but benefits depend on schemes yet to be fully operational. And the tripartite system, which BMS regards as the proper place to settle disputes, awaits revival. None of this can be settled by announcements alone. It needs patient representation, well-prepared data, and the work of karyakartas in every district.

We wish the new team well. A union grows when karyakartas of every region find a place in it, and when its leaders remember that they speak for the worker at the last gate of the last factory.
